One wordmark, set in soft lowercase letterforms. It is the whole of the chimie logo.

There is no separate symbol, monogram or stacked version. The wordmark is used everywhere as delivered: indigo on lavender, white or lavender over photography. Always use the supplied artwork; never retype it.
The wordmark is drawn, not typed: rounded strokes, open counters and a dotted pair of i’s. Its letterforms echo E8888 Web, the headline face, which is why the two sit comfortably together on posters.

Keep a clear zone of X on every side, where X is the height of the wordmark. In the source files the wordmark sits 2X from the page edge on business-plan pages (15 px mark, 30 px margin) and about 1.6X on posters (37 px mark, 59 px margin).

Documents use indigo on lavender. Over photography the wordmark turns white (posters) or lavender (business plan), see 2.5. Lavender on indigo and indigo on white are recommended extensions and not yet in use. Never place the wordmark on a colour outside the palette.

A quiet palette: deep indigo type on a soft lavender ground, with photography doing the rest.
chimie uses two colours. Lavender covers every business-plan page; indigo carries all type, rules and the wordmark. On posters the photograph is the ground and type turns white.
Indigo and lavender are the brand. Indigo on lavender passes AAA contrast (7.95 : 1).

White is used for type and the wordmark over photography. Dusk is a derived tint (indigo mixed 20% toward lavender) for captions and secondary text; it is a recommendation, not found in the source files.
Indigo 700 is the brand indigo. Darker steps are for pressed states and deep backgrounds; lighter steps for tints, charts and hover fills. The ramp is generated; only the base step is measured.

Lavender 200 is the brand lavender. Darker steps run toward indigo, so the two families meet in the middle. Use the light end for panels on white. The ramp is generated; only the base step is measured.
Every shade tested against lavender and indigo. “Aa” shows the text colour that passes 4.5 : 1 on that cell. Body text needs 4.5 : 1, large text 3 : 1.

Measured by area across the 21 business-plan pages: lavender ground about 62%, photography about 32%, indigo about 6% (type, rules and shapes; layers overlap, so treat these as approximate). Posters are 100% photography with white type.
Three grounds cover every application. Lavender for documents, indigo for emphasis pages and dividers (recommended), photography for posters, with white type.
Two faces: E8888 Web for poster headlines, Inter for everything else. Lowercase on posters.

E8888 Web is a soft, rounded sans that echoes the wordmark; Inter does the reading work in Regular, Medium and Bold. Two supporting faces also appear in the business plan: Editorial New for folios and Favorit Mono Std for sources and chart labels.
Display face. Used at 50 px for poster headlines and event descriptions, always in lowercase, white over photography. One weight, Regular.
Text face. Regular for body copy (20 px on business-plan pages), Medium for section headings and poster RSVP lines (30 px), Bold for paragraph lead-ins.

Every size here is measured from the source files. “auto” means the files use automatic line height. Editorial New and Favorit Mono Std are not installed on this machine, so they are listed but not shown.

Two treatments: full-colour film on posters, indigo duotone in documents.

Most images in the source files are film scans (their filenames are lab frame numbers): warm, soft colour, visible grain and real moments from scent clubs and workshops. In the business plan the same kind of photograph is delivered as an indigo duotone, baked into the image file rather than applied in Figma.

Posters keep the film’s own colour: warm and slightly faded, with soft contrast. Documents map the image to indigo, from deep indigo shadows to lavender-white highlights, so photographs sit inside the palette.
Pick images with a calm area for type and the wordmark. Natural light, real hands and real objects, people mid-conversation rather than posing. Full colour for posters; indigo duotone for documents.
Full colour: a scent club table mid-conversation, in natural light

The same scent club photograph, pushed in the wrong directions. Don’t boost saturation, cool the image down, blow out the highlights or crush the shadows; keep the film’s own softness.

Three posters add Figma noise on top of the photograph: Monotone, size 0.5, 25% on the image and 15% on the whole frame. Use it to unify photos from different sources. Leave it off when the scan already shows grain.
Generous space, small type, and photographs that run to the edge.
Documents are 2000 × 1125 px landscape pages; posters are 1215 × 1519 px portrait (4 : 5). Both keep text small and push it to the edges, leaving the image or the lavender ground to breathe.

Five columns on a 2000 px page: 20 px margins and gutters, 376 px columns. The grid is attached to three pages only, so treat it as guidance. Text blocks are usually 578 px wide, and x = 1208, the start of column 4, is the most common text anchor.

The perfume industry, often perceived as intimidating and exclusive, leaves many curious individuals underserved. Traditional fragrance houses have long dominated the market, associating scent with luxury, complex terminology, and high price points. This has created a barrier for many who are interested in exploring the world of perfume but feel excluded by its elitist nature.

However, there is a noticeable shift occurring in the industry, with a growing interest in more personalized, meaningful, and accessible sensory experiences.
Consumers are increasingly seeking ways to express themselves through scent, using it as a medium for self-discovery, emotional connection, and creativity. This shift is also fueled by a broader trend where people crave deeper

connections with the products they consume, seeking 
authenticity and individuality over mass-market offerings. According to a 2023 report from Statista, the global fragrance and flavour industry is projected to reach $52.3 billion by 2025, up from $49.4 billion in 2023, indicating growing consumer interest in this sector

Through chimie, scent exploration becomes accessible and approachable, demystifying the world of fragrance. By offering a blend of education, creativity, and high-quality niche products, chimie bridges the gap between traditional perfume culture and the modern desire for personalized olfactory experiences. Through workshops, scent clubs, and one-on-one consultations, chimie empowers individuals to connect with their senses in ways that are both educational and inspiring.

This approach aligns with the broader rise of niche fragrances, 
which are gaining popularity as consumers move away from mass-market perfumes in favour of unique, artisanal scents that reflect their individual identities. As highlighted by Business of Fashion, niche fragrance brands are experiencing a surge in demand, driven by consumers' increasing desire for quality, storytelling, and exclusivity

. The industry’s shift towards smaller, independent perfumers aligns with chimie’s mission to offer curated, meaningful scent experiences that foster a sense of connection and creativity, all while making the world of fragrance more inclusive.

Jean-Julien (JJ) is a swiss knife creative. Graphic designer to the core, he brings over 10 years of experience to chimie, where his focus is to amplify projects that are steering the world towards a better future. At chimie, he translates Heather’s vision through art direction, photography, and design, strategically shaping a visual identity that drives engagement and growth.

Claudia is a seasoned PR and marketing consultant. With a strong background in design writing, she collaborates closely with clients to elevate their brands and public profiles. Specializing in crafting personalized strategies, Claudia focuses on areas such as press relations, brand storytelling, social media, and copywriting. Her expertise extends to building compelling founder profiles, crafting impactful PR campaigns, and enhancing brand visibility ensuring that each creative vision is showcased effectively to the right audience.
Marianne Beausjour, Fragrance consultant & Workshop Facilitator

Marianne is a fragrance consultant with a background in fashion Marketing. She blends her passion for scent with a strategic approach to client engagement, known for her exceptional sales skills and ability to build lasting relationships. At Chimie, she leads immersive workshops that guide individuals and groups through the art of scent discovery, helping them deepen their connection to fragrance. Marianne is also set to play a key role in our upcoming brick-and-mortar location.

Heather is the founder of chimie, bringing a unique blend of operations expertise and a passion for scent to the business. As a natural community builder and operations leader, she brings a unique skill set to chimie, ensuring that every aspect of the business runs smoothly, efficiently, and strategically. With extensive experience in building businesses from the ground up, Heather was the first employee at Kotn, now a multi-million-dollar company, where she played an instrumental role in shaping its rapid growth. Her expertise in streamlining operations and scaling businesses is foundational to chimie’s success.
